questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
questions.solution: The library is contrasted with shops and malls, where a visitor is **expected** to buy. 'Forbidden to buy' and 'excused to buy' make no sense here, and 'prevent' takes 'from', not 'to'.
questions.shortcut: Library vs mall contrast: nobody expects you to spend.
questions.passage: A town's public library is often the last place where anyone may sit for hours without being (1) ___ to buy something. Students preparing for competitive examinations crowd its reading rooms because their homes are too small and too noisy for serious study. Yet in many districts these libraries are (2) ___ for want of funds: roofs leak, newspapers arrive late, and the shelves hold books that no one has asked for in decades. Reviving them would not be (3) ___. A modest budget for new titles, reliable electricity and longer opening hours would (4) ___ transform them. A library that stays open until late evening serves the young clerk who can study only after work, and it (5) ___ the town something no shopping mall can: a quiet public room that belongs to everyone.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
questions.solution: 'For want of funds' and the list that follows (leaking roofs, late newspapers, stale shelves) describe decline — the libraries are **languishing** (weakening from neglect). Flourishing and multiplying are the reverse; competing has no support in the passage.
questions.shortcut: Colon test: the list after the colon describes the blank — decay.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
questions.solution: The next sentence speaks of a **modest budget**, so the writer is saying revival would not be **expensive**. 'Not necessary', 'not possible' and 'not useful' all contradict the writer, who clearly wants the libraries revived.
questions.shortcut: The sentence after the blank ('modest budget') defines it.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (4).
questions.solution: The writer argues that small spending would make a big difference, so the measures would **substantially** transform the libraries. Scarcely and rarely would reverse the argument; 'reluctantly' gives feelings to a budget, which makes no sense.
questions.shortcut: Positive argument → positive-degree adverb; scarcely/rarely are negative words.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (5).
questions.solution: The library **offers** the town what no mall can (offer): a free, quiet public room. 'Denies' reverses the praise; 'charges the town something' is about payment; 'borrows' makes the library take instead of give.
questions.shortcut: The colon shows the good thing the library gives → offers.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

CANDID
questions.solution: Candid means open and honest in speech — **frank**. Secretive is the opposite; 'sweet' is a sound trap (candy); cautious describes guarded speech, the reverse of candid.
questions.shortcut: candid = can't hide: a candid remark / candid photo (unposed, natural).

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

EPHEMERAL
questions.solution: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time; its opposite is **permanent**. Transient and fleeting are synonyms (the classic trap), and delicate describes fragility, not duration.
questions.shortcut: Two options mean the same as the word? Both are synonyms — strike them and pick the opposite.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To cry over spilt milk
options: to regret something that cannot be undone
questions.solution: Once milk is spilt it cannot be put back, so crying over it is useless: the idiom means **to regret what cannot be undone**. The other three are literal readings of the words.
questions.shortcut: Idioms are never literal — cancel every option that talks about real milk or tears.

questions.q: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution: **Accommodate** has double c AND double m: ac-com-mo-date. Accomodate drops an m, Acommodate drops a c, and Accommodete changes the ending.
questions.shortcut: It is big enough to accommodate two c's and two m's.

questions.q: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution: **Conscientious** = conscience + -tious: con-sci-en-tious. Conscientous drops the i before -ous, Consciencious uses c for t, and Concientious loses the s of 'sci'.
questions.shortcut: Build it from science: con + SCIEN + tious.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate one word for the given expression.

Handwriting that cannot be read
questions.solution: **Illegible** (il + legible, from Latin *legere*, to read) means impossible to read. Ineligible means not qualified; illiterate describes a person who cannot read; invisible means cannot be seen.
questions.shortcut: legible → read (as in 'lecture'); eligible → choose. Don't mix them.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

He has been living in this city ___ 2015.
questions.solution: A perfect-continuous tense with a **point** of time takes **since**: since 2015. 'For' is used with a period (for ten years); 'from' needs a 'to/till'; 'by' marks a deadline.
questions.shortcut: Point of time → since; period of time → for.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Despite repeated failures, she remained ___ and kept working towards her goal.
questions.solution: 'Despite failures ... kept working' needs a word meaning **not discouraged** — undeterred. Uninterested and undecided clash with 'kept working towards her goal'; unprepared has nothing to do with failures.
questions.shortcut: 'Despite' + 'kept working' → a word for not giving up.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

Each of the students (a) have submitted (b) the assignment on time (c) No error (d)
questions.solution: The subject is **each**, which is singular; 'of the students' only describes it. So the verb must be singular: 'Each of the students **has** submitted...'.
questions.shortcut: Each / every / either / neither + of + plural → singular verb.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

Being a rainy day, (a) the school was closed (b) earlier than usual (c) No error (d)
questions.solution: As written, 'Being a rainy day' seems to describe 'the school', which is illogical — a school is not a rainy day. An impersonal subject is needed: '**It being** a rainy day, the school was closed...'. The error is in part (a).
questions.shortcut: Participle phrase must describe the next subject; if it can't, add 'It'.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to replace the bold part of the sentence.

No sooner did the bell ring **when the students rushed out**.
questions.solution: 'No sooner' is always paired with **than**: 'No sooner did the bell ring than the students rushed out.' 'When' belongs with hardly/scarcely; 'then' and 'as' cannot complete the comparison.
questions.shortcut: No sooner → than; Hardly/Scarcely → when.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Who wrote this letter?
options: By whom was this letter written?
By whom this letter was written?
By whom has this letter been written?
By whom is this letter written?
questions.solution: In the passive, 'who' becomes **by whom**, and the question keeps the helping verb before the subject: By whom **was** this letter written? B misses the question order; C changes the tense to present perfect; D changes it to simple present.
questions.shortcut: who → by whom; past simple → was/were + V3; keep question word order.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The teacher said to the students, "Do not make a noise."
options: The teacher said the students not to make a noise.
The teacher told to the students not to make a noise.
The teacher told the students not to make a noise.
The teacher told the students that do not make a noise.
questions.solution: A negative command becomes **told/ordered + object + not to + V1**. B keeps the imperative after 'that'; C uses 'said' with a direct object; D wrongly puts 'to' after told.
questions.shortcut: Negative imperative → not to + V1; 'said to' → told (no 'to').

questions.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful passage.

**1.** Ravi opened a savings account with his first salary. **P:** Within two years the small deposits had grown into a useful sum. **Q:** He decided to put aside a fixed amount every month. **R:** When his mother fell ill, he paid for her treatment without borrowing. **S:** Some months it was hard, but he never missed a deposit. **6.** Thrift, he realised, is a form of freedom.
questions.solution: **Q** (the decision to save) follows the account opening → **S** (the effort month after month) → **P** (the result after two years) → **R** (the pay-off when his mother fell ill) → S6's lesson. S cannot come first because 'it' in S needs the saving plan from Q.
questions.shortcut: Plan → effort → result → pay-off.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

If you had left home on time, you ___ the train yesterday.
questions.solution: 'If + had + V3' is the third conditional (an unreal past), so the main clause takes **would have + V3**. 'Yesterday' rules out would catch / will catch, and 'had caught' cannot be the result clause.
questions.shortcut: had + V3 ↔ would have + V3.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Electronic devices are too dangerous to be repaired by anyone other than the manufacturer.
Consumers today simply prefer new gadgets to repaired ones.
Neighbourhood repairmen should be trained by phone companies.
Manufacturers' design and pricing choices discourage repair, and fair access to parts and manuals can help reverse this.
questions.solution: Paragraph 1 blames design choices, paragraph 2 blames repair pricing, and paragraph 3 offers the fix (fair access to parts, tools and manuals). B turns the companies' partial excuse into the thesis; C is directly denied ('not an accident of consumer taste'); D is never proposed.
questions.shortcut: Thesis = problem (paras 1-2) + remedy (para 3).
questions.passage:
A generation ago, a broken radio went to the neighbourhood repairman, who opened it, found the faulty part and charged a small fee. Today a phone with a cracked screen or a tired battery is more likely to be thrown into a drawer and replaced. The change is not an accident of consumer taste. Many manufacturers glue batteries in place, use screws that ordinary tools cannot turn, and refuse to sell spare parts or repair manuals to independent shops. Some even link each part to the device's serial number through software, so that a genuine replacement screen fitted by an outsider triggers warnings or stops working altogether.

Companies defend these practices on grounds of safety and quality. A poorly fitted battery, they argue, can overheat, and an untrained technician can damage waterproof seals. There is some truth in this, but critics point out that the same companies earn handsomely from authorised repairs priced close to the cost of a new device. When repair costs nearly as much as replacement, most buyers choose replacement, and the discarded devices add to a mountain of electronic waste that grows every year.

The 'right to repair' movement asks for something modest: that owners and independent repairers be able to buy parts, tools and manuals at fair prices. Several governments have begun to listen, requiring manufacturers to supply spare parts for a fixed number of years. Such rules will not end the throwaway habit on their own, but they restore an old idea that had begun to seem quaint — that a thing you have paid for is truly yours to mend.

questions.q: According to the passage, some manufacturers link each part to the device's serial number so that —
options: spare parts become cheaper for independent shops
a genuine replacement part fitted by an outsider may trigger warnings or stop working
stolen phones can be traced by the police
questions.solution: The passage says the link means 'a genuine replacement screen fitted by an outsider triggers warnings or stops working altogether'. The other options are never mentioned.
questions.shortcut: Detail question: find 'serial number' and read the 'so that' clause.

questions.q: Why, according to the passage, do most buyers choose replacement over repair?
options: Because independent shops refuse to repair phones
Because governments encourage the purchase of new devices
Because authorised repair often costs nearly as much as a new device
Because new devices are safer than repaired ones
questions.solution: 'When repair costs nearly as much as replacement, most buyers choose replacement.' B repeats the companies' argument, not buyers' reasoning; C reverses the facts (companies refuse to supply the shops); D contradicts paragraph 3.
questions.shortcut: Match the cause–effect sentence: repair ≈ new price → replace.

questions.q: The word 'quaint', as used in the passage, most nearly means —
questions.solution: The idea that you may mend what you own had begun to seem **old-fashioned** — something from 'a generation ago'. Quaint means attractively unusual or old-fashioned; it carries no sense of danger, cost or illegality.
questions.shortcut: Link the word to the passage's time contrast: 'a generation ago' vs 'today'.

questions.q: How does the author treat the companies' safety argument?
options: As irrelevant to the question of repair
As partly valid but not the whole story
questions.solution: 'There is some truth in this, **but** critics point out...' — the author grants the argument some weight and then shows the profit motive behind it. B ignores the 'but'; C ignores 'some truth'; D is wrong because the argument is about repair itself.
questions.shortcut: 'Some truth ... but' = partial agreement: choose the balanced option.
